blurb: Where everyday words and phrases really came from

questions.q: 'Kindergarten' comes from German. What does it literally mean?
questions.fact: Educator Friedrich Froebel coined the name in 1840 for his school in Germany.
questions.src: etymonline.com kindergarten (lit. children-garden; Froebel coined it 1840)

questions.q: The 'wiki' in Wikipedia comes from a Hawaiian word meaning what?
questions.fact: Ward Cunningham named his 1995 WikiWikiWeb after the Wiki Wiki Shuttle buses at Honolulu's airport.
questions.src: Wikipedia History of wikis (WikiWikiWeb 25 Mar 1995; wiki = quick; Wiki Wiki Shuttle, Honolulu airport)

questions.q: In the Japanese word 'emoji,' what does the 'e' mean?
questions.fact: Moji means character, so the resemblance to the English word emotion is pure coincidence.
questions.src: wordorigins.org emoji (e = picture, moji = character; unrelated to emotion)

questions.q: 'Shampoo' comes from a Hindi word that originally meant what?
questions.fact: In English it first meant a massage (1762); the hair-washing sense arrived around 1860.
questions.src: etymonline.com shampoo (Hindi champo < champna 'to press, knead'; massage 1762; hair-washing 1860)

questions.q: The phrase 'saved by the bell' comes from which sport?
questions.fact: It's 19th-century boxing slang. The popular tale about bells on coffins has no evidence behind it.
questions.src: phrases.org.uk saved-by-the-bell (late-19th-c. boxing slang, earliest found Feb 1893; no evidence for coffin story)

questions.q: 'Jump the shark' traces to a 1977 episode of which TV show?
questions.fact: Fonzie jumped a shark on water skis; the phrase for a show past its peak caught on in the late 1990s.
questions.src: Wikipedia Jumping the shark (Happy Days S5E3 aired 20 Sep 1977; coined 1985; JumptheShark.com 1997)

questions.q: 'Cut to the chase' comes from which field?
questions.fact: Early silent films often ended in a chase, and the phrase shows up as a script direction by 1929.
questions.src: phrases.org.uk cut-to-the-chase (silent-era chase endings; 'Cut to chase' script direction in 1929 novel Hollywood Girl)

questions.q: 'Steal my thunder' traces to John Dennis, who heard his new stage thunder effect used in which play?
questions.fact: Dennis had devised the effect for his own play, Appius and Virginia, which closed quickly.
questions.src: Wikipedia Stealing thunder; quoteinvestigator.com 2015/12/23/thunder; phrases.org.uk steal-ones-thunder (all name Macbeth; Appius and Virginia failed/closed quickly; play's year differs 1704 vs 1709, so year omitted)

questions.q: The word 'nerd' is often traced to a 1950 children's book by which author?
questions.fact: In If I Ran the Zoo, a nerd is one of the odd creatures; the slang sense appears by 1951.
questions.src: merriam-webster.com nerd (perhaps from If I Ran the Zoo, 1950; first known use 1951)

questions.q: The earliest known use of 'selfie' was a 2002 online post from which country?
questions.fact: Oxford Dictionaries later named selfie its Word of the Year for 2013.
questions.src: SBS News 2013 (earliest known use: 2002 post on ABC online forum, Australia; Oxford WotY 2013)

questions.q: The word 'robot' comes from a 1920 play written in which language?
questions.fact: Karel Čapek credited his brother Josef with the word, from the Czech robota, forced labor.
questions.src: etymonline.com robot (R.U.R. 1920, Czech; robota forced labor; Josef Capek credited); wording softened from 'debuted' because one etymology claims an earlier Josef short story

questions.q: 'Serendipity' comes from Serendip, an old name for which island nation?
questions.fact: Horace Walpole coined it in a 1754 letter, inspired by the fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip.
questions.src: Wikipedia Serendipity (Walpole to Mann 28 Jan 1754; Three Princes of Serendip; Serendip = Persian name for Sri Lanka)
